avebury.name: Avebury henge
facts: Avebury is a Neolithic henge monument in Wiltshire containing three stone circles.
It contains the largest megalithic stone circle in Britain.
It was built and altered over several centuries in the third millennium BC.
The village of Avebury lies partly inside the henge.
It is part of the Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites UNESCO World Heritage Site and is cared for by the National Trust and English Heritage.

birdoswald.name: Birdoswald Roman Fort
facts: Birdoswald is a Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall in Cumbria.
Its Roman name was Banna.
A long stretch of the Wall survives near the fort.
It is in the care of English Heritage.
Hadrian's Wall is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire UNESCO World Heritage Site.

durrington.name: Durrington Walls
facts: Durrington Walls is a large Neolithic henge about 3 km north-east of Stonehenge.
It dates to around 2500 BC.
Excavations from 2004 to 2007 by the Stonehenge Riverside Project found evidence of a large settlement.
Some archaeologists suggest it housed the people who built Stonehenge.
It is owned by the National Trust and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site.

giza-pyramids.name: Giza pyramid complex
facts: The Giza pyramid complex is on the Giza Plateau near Cairo, Egypt.
It includes the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, built during the Fourth Dynasty of the Old Kingdom.
The Great Pyramid of Khufu was completed around 2560 BC.
The Great Pyramid is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one largely intact.
It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Memphis and its Necropolis', inscribed in 1979.

housesteads.name: Housesteads Roman Fort
facts: Housesteads is a Roman auxiliary fort on Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland.
Its Roman name is generally thought to have been Vercovicium.
It was built around AD 124, shortly after work on the Wall began in AD 122.
Its remains include barracks, granaries and well-preserved latrines.
Hadrian's Wall is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire UNESCO World Heritage Site.

silbury.name: Silbury Hill
facts: Silbury Hill is a prehistoric artificial chalk mound near Avebury in Wiltshire.
At about 30 metres high, it is the tallest prehistoric human-made mound in Europe.
It was built around 2400 BC, in the late Neolithic.
Its purpose remains unknown; excavations have found no burial.
Public access to the hill itself is not permitted, to protect it.

sphinx.name: Great Sphinx of Giza
facts: The Great Sphinx of Giza is a limestone statue of a reclining sphinx on the Giza Plateau.
It is commonly thought to have been made for the pharaoh Khafre, of the Fourth Dynasty.
It is one of the largest and oldest monumental sculptures in the world.
It was carved from the bedrock of the plateau.
It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Memphis and its Necropolis'.

stonehenge.name: Stonehenge
facts: Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England.
It consists of an outer ring of large sarsen stones topped by lintels, with smaller bluestones set within.
Construction took place in several phases, from around 3000 BC to around 2000 BC.
The bluestones are thought to have been brought from the Preseli Hills in west Wales.
Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
It is managed by English Heritage and is a scheduled monument.

vindolanda.name: Vindolanda
facts: Vindolanda is a Roman auxiliary fort just south of Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland.
Its earliest forts predate the Wall itself.
It is famous for the Vindolanda tablets, wooden writing tablets from around the late 1st and early 2nd centuries AD.
The tablets are among the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain.
The site is run by the Vindolanda Trust and excavation continues there.

west-kennet.name: West Kennet Long Barrow
facts: West Kennet Long Barrow is a Neolithic chambered tomb near Silbury Hill in Wiltshire.
It was constructed around 3650 BC.
Excavations found the remains of at least several dozen people in its chambers.
The entrance was later blocked with large sarsen stones.
It is in the care of English Heritage and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site.

woodhenge.name: Woodhenge
facts: Woodhenge is a Neolithic henge and timber circle just south of Durrington Walls.
It was identified from aerial photography in 1925.
It was excavated by Maud and Benjamin Cunnington in the late 1920s.
Concrete markers now show the positions of the original timber posts.
It is in the care of English Heritage.
